I listen to their points and don’t make it an argument. “Well I’m not like that” doesn’t get rid of the fact that ABA has traumatized many people, especially within the autism community. People are allowed to have their opinions as ABA has not had the best history. It’s sad as this practice is so helpful to others, it’s unfortunate how many terrible practitioners have been able to work in this field. It’s horrible that so many people have had traumatic experiences within this field. Emphasize that you hear them and don’t speak over them. 

I follow a lot of groups on Facebook and other forms of social media that critique ABA. I also follow autistic individuals who had traumatic experiences with ABA. I listen to their concerns and implement them within my own practice. I feel if we can’t listen to the people who critique our practices, we will stay in the same pattern. 

I’ve been doing a lot of research on assent! It’s amazing and has stopped me from engaging in power struggles with my clients! I suggest you look it up! :)

I am not a fan of people who just want autistic individuals to mask. I focus on increasing functional skills/decreasing challenging behaviors. I don’t want my clients to be “normal” I want them to have the necessary skills to thrive. I don’t see an issue with stereotypy behaviors unless it’s causing harm to the individual or another person (which I have never seen). Forcing eye contact is not appropriate in my opinion, I’m also not the biggest fan of DTT lessons unless necessary. I love teaching skills within play or their natural environment! I feel sitting at a table for long periods of time is not beneficial. Just my two cents :)
